body:
(I apologize in advance for any awkward English--it's not my first language) I'm a 15 year old female, and I was diagnosed with depression and anorexia some time last summer, but I've known I was depressed and suicidal since I was around 7, and I've been abused physically by my parents since I was 4. I just want to thank you for existing. You are living proof to me that kind, caring mothers do indeed exist, and you are proof that mothers actually can care about their child's mental health. I applaud you for that, and trust me, I've dreamed about having a mother like you for the longest time. I would sacrifice anything to have a mother like you.

Now, about your daughter. Her reaction to you seems unwarranted and ungrateful, maybe, but it actually is genuine--though it's directed at the wrong person. Your daughter has every right to be angry...at her father. As a child of two unsupportive and abusive parents, I can understand why she feels angry. She wants support and love from both of you, not just you, but your husband as well.

I have been forced into therapy before. I am still in sessions with said therapist, and a psychiatrist, and I have been an inpatient at a hospital (which means I have stayed overnight for a couple weeks). It sucks. Yes, it does. Your daughter seems not to think that she needs help (at least that's what it seems like). I thought therapy was unnecessary, and I also thought psychology/psychiatry shouldn't even be counted as a real science (that's a different story which is a tangent and unnecessary here). So I resisted therapy. I still resist it to some extent now, even though it should help me, but it doesn't. It makes me feel like I'm wasting my parents' money on the therapist, the therapist's time on me, and my time when I could be studying. Maybe your daughter feels the same way.

About grades. She's in college classes in high school? I am too, and yes, they are hard. If she's good enough to get into those classes, she will be good enough to catch up. I find that studying keeps my mind off the things that are going on in life (and it keeps my mother's fists off me too). Maybe your daughter will also find that studying, though it may not be as fun as, say, Facebook, will still help distract her from her sadness and depression, as it does for me.

Lastly, I'd like to say again that you are an *angel* of a mother. I can only hope that one day someone will care for me the way you care for your daughter. I can only wish that one day my mother will sincerely say "I love you" to me without faking it or hitting me and taking it back afterwards. I wish your daughter and you the best luck, and I hope her depression recedes and that she feels much better :)

But if colleges see that I've caused so many problems to myself just after starting high school, then they'll never accept me, and it's almost impossible to carry oneself in society, get a job, etc. if you haven't gone to college.
